subtype: Holding arms close to the body [Expressing]
passage:
On his first morning at the playgroup in Nairobi, Kaito stood by the door with his arms pressed tight against his sides, hands tucked under his armpits. He watched the other children banging drums but did not move.

Teacher Wanjiru didn't pull him in. She put a small drum near his father's chair and went back to the circle.

Kaito's father sat down. After a while Kaito leaned on his father's knee. Then one hand came out and tapped the drum, very softly.

qa.q: Where did Teacher Wanjiru put the small drum?
qa.a: Near his father's chair.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling as he stood by the door with his arms pressed to his sides?
qa.a: He was most likely shy and cautious in a new place full of strangers. He might also have been curious, since he kept watching the drums.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Wanjiru gave Kaito time and left the drum near his father instead of pulling him in, so he could join at his own pace with a familiar adult close by.

qa.q: What would change if Wanjiru had pulled Kaito into the circle?
qa.a: He might have become more frightened and kept his arms tucked even tighter, taking longer to feel safe.

grounding: It shows a shy child keeping his arms tucked in around new people and loosening up with time and a familiar adult nearby.

passage:
The kite was torn right down the middle. The neighbour's goat had trampled it in the field behind the house.

Anand stood over it, fists clenched so tight his knuckles went pale. His face turned red.

Anjali Didi knelt beside him. "You're so angry. You worked hard on that kite." She pulled a soft cloth ball from her pocket, the one they used for catch. "Squeeze this as hard as you want."

Anand squeezed and squeezed. Then he threw it at the fence. "Stupid goat!"

"Yes," Didi said. "Stupid goat. Tomorrow we'll make a new one."

qa.q: What had trampled the kite?
qa.a: The neighbour's goat.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he clenched his fists?
qa.a: He was most likely angry and frustrated that his kite was ruined; his pale knuckles and red face show how strong it was. He may also have felt sad about the lost work.

qa.q: How did Anjali Didi help Anand with his anger?
qa.a: She named the feeling, gave him a soft ball to squeeze as a safe outlet, and offered a plan to make a new kite.

qa.q: If you were Anjali Didi, what would you want Anand to learn?
qa.a: That big angry feelings are allowed, and that there are safe ways to let them out, like squeezing a ball, instead of hitting.

grounding: It shows a preschooler clenching his fists in anger and an older sister offering words and a soft ball as a safe outlet.

passage:
Monday: at story circle, Sabina drummed her fingers on the floor, tap-tap-tap. "Stop fidgeting," Reena Ma'am said. Sabina stopped, and stared out of the window instead.

Wednesday: Reena Ma'am watched Sabina doing a jigsaw. Her fingers drummed on the table the whole time, and she finished before anyone else.

Friday: at story circle, Reena Ma'am handed Sabina a squishy star to hold. Sabina squeezed it through the whole story, then told it back almost word for word.

qa.q: What did Reena Ma'am hand Sabina on Friday?
qa.a: A squishy star to hold.

qa.q: What might Sabina's finger-drumming at story circle have meant?
qa.a: She might have been bored or restless, but the jigsaw on Wednesday suggests the drumming also helped her concentrate. On Monday, stopping seemed to make her lose interest.

qa.q: What changed Reena Ma'am's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: Watching Sabina drum while she focused on the jigsaw showed the fidgeting was helping, so a squishy star let her keep moving without distracting others.

qa.q: How would Sabina experience story time if the scolding had continued?
qa.a: She might have felt told off for something that helped her, and kept drifting off to the window instead of following the story.

grounding: It shows a child's finger-drumming that could be boredom or focus, and an adult watching the context instead of scolding.

passage:
Sports day at the school, and the lemon-and-spoon race was next. Pooja stood at the line with both hands behind her back, fingers crossed so hard they hurt.

"Why are your fingers like that?" asked a boy beside her.

"For luck," Pooja said.

Across the field, Damini tugged her own left ear twice. Pooja grinned and tugged hers back. It was their secret sign: meet at the swings after.

Pooja's lemon fell halfway. She laughed, picked it up and walked the rest.

qa.q: What was their secret sign?
qa.a: Tugging the left ear twice, which meant meet at the swings after.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling as she crossed her fingers so hard they hurt?
qa.a: She was likely nervous and hopeful about the race. The grin when Damini tugged her ear shows she also felt happy and close to her friend.

qa.q: What makes the secret sign work between Pooja and Damini?
qa.a: They both know what the ear tug means, so it is a private, playful message that others around them would not understand.

qa.q: How does the boy beside Pooja see her crossed fingers?
qa.a: He doesn't know the custom and is curious, so he asks why her fingers look like that.

grounding: It shows a child crossing her fingers for luck and sharing a secret ear-tug sign that only her friend understands.

passage:
Sunday: Dadi arrived, and Mummy pushed Alka's hands together. "Say namaste properly!" Alka pulled away and hid behind the curtain.

The next Friday: Mummy didn't push. She simply greeted Dadi warmly, hands folded, smiling. When Asif Chacha from downstairs brought sweets, she thanked him and he touched his hand to his heart. Alka watched from the sofa.

The Sunday after: Alka ran to the door, folded her hands for Dadi, then turned and put a hand on her chest for Asif Chacha. Both of them beamed.

qa.q: What did Asif Chacha bring on Friday?
qa.a: Sweets.

qa.q: Why did Alka hide behind the curtain on the first Sunday?
qa.a: She most likely felt embarrassed and upset at being pushed into a greeting, so she pulled away. She may also have been shy after not seeing Dadi for a while.

qa.q: What worked better than pushing Alka's hands together?
qa.a: Mummy simply greeted people warmly herself, so Alka could watch and copy the gestures when she was ready.

qa.q: How do Dadi and Asif Chacha feel when Alka greets them on her own?
qa.a: They beam, so they feel pleased and touched that the greeting came from her, each in their own style.

grounding: It shows a preschooler learning namaste and a hand-on-heart greeting through warm modelling rather than force.

passage:
The library in Utrecht was warm and quiet. Bilal found a book about tractors and shouted, "Look! A red one!"

Jana, the librarian, looked up from her desk and put a finger to her lips.

Bilal froze. His hands tightened on the book. Then he looked at her face properly. She was smiling, eyebrows raised, and she pointed at a man asleep in the armchair.

Bilal grinned and put his own finger to his lips. He tiptoed over and whispered, "A red one." Jana gave him a thumbs up.

qa.q: What did Bilal find a book about?
qa.a: About tractors.

qa.q: Why did Bilal freeze when Jana put a finger to her lips?
qa.a: He probably felt worried that he was in trouble for shouting. Once he saw her smiling face, he felt reassured that she only wanted quiet.

qa.q: How did Bilal work out what the gesture meant?
qa.a: He looked at Jana's face and where she pointed, which showed she was friendly and simply asking for quiet for the sleeping man.

qa.q: How does Jana feel about Bilal's excitement?
qa.a: She seems warm about it, smiling and giving a thumbs up, while still keeping the library quiet.

grounding: It shows a preschooler reading a finger-to-lips request for quiet in a library and checking the adult's face before assuming trouble.

passage:
Five minutes before home time, the rain was so loud on the tin roof that Elizabeth Miss had to shout the spelling words.

Tarun's hand shot up. He wiggled it. He bounced on his seat. He did not call out, though his face was scrunched with the effort.

Elizabeth Miss was bent over another child's slate. Tarun's hand wobbled; he crossed his legs.

At last she looked up, saw him, and gave a quick nod towards the door. Tarun ran for the toilet.

When he came back, she gave him a thumbs up. "Good waiting."

qa.q: How loud was the rain on the tin roof?
qa.a: So loud that Elizabeth Miss had to shout the spelling words.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling while his hand wobbled and he crossed his legs?
qa.a: He was likely uncomfortable and anxious because he urgently needed the toilet, and frustrated by the wait. His scrunched face also shows he was proud to try hard not to call out.

qa.q: What helped end Tarun's frustration quickly?
qa.a: A quick nod towards the door from Elizabeth Miss let him go at once, and her "Good waiting" afterwards praised his effort.

qa.q: What would change if Elizabeth Miss had not looked up for a long time?
qa.a: Tarun might have given up waiting and shouted out, or had an accident, and felt upset about it.

grounding: It shows a child raising his hand and waiting instead of blurting out, and a teacher's quick nod easing the strain.

passage:
The wedding hall was so noisy that nobody could hear Mridul. He tugged Keerthana Athai's sari and tipped an invisible cup to his mouth.

"Juice?" she guessed. He shook his head and did it again, slower.

"Water!" He nodded.

When she came back, he gripped an invisible steering wheel and turned it, then pointed at the door.

"You want to go home?" He nodded, then hid his face in her sari.

"Shall we tell Amma together?" she asked. He took her hand.

qa.q: What did Mridul tug to get Keerthana Athai's attention?
qa.a: Keerthana Athai's sari.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he hid his face in her sari?
qa.a: He was probably tired and shy, maybe overwhelmed by the noisy hall, and embarrassed about asking to go home. He relied on mime and on her guessing because he felt too shy to push further.

qa.q: How did Keerthana Athai help Mridul when words failed?
qa.a: She kept guessing his mimes, checked with him each time, and offered to tell Amma together so he didn't have to speak up alone.

qa.q: What would change if the hall were quiet?
qa.a: Mridul might still mime because he is shy, but he could have been heard more easily if he tried to speak.

grounding: It shows a preschooler miming drinking and driving to explain himself in a noisy hall and a shy child relying on an adult to guess.

passage:
Back in the colony after the weekend at the lake, Pema stretched her arms as wide as they could go. "The fish was THIS big!"

Kashish laughed. "That's bigger than you!"

"Almost," Pema said. She let her arms come in a tiny bit. "Papa caught it. And we caught more." She held up three fingers, then looked at them, frowned and folded one down. "Two. One jumped back in."

"Was the first one really that big?"

Pema grinned and spread her arms wide again. "Bigger!"

qa.q: How many fingers did Pema hold up at first?
qa.a: Three fingers.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she spread her arms wide again and said "Bigger!"?
qa.a: She was most likely excited and proud about the fishing trip, and her wide arms showed that excitement more than the fish's real size. She may also have enjoyed teasing Kashish a little.

qa.q: How could an adult respond to Pema's big fish gesture?
qa.a: They could enjoy the excitement with her, and maybe ask something playful, like whether it was bigger than the table, without insisting on exact size.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Pema's story?
qa.a: Kashish finds it funny and doubts the size, laughing that it is bigger than Pema, but still wants to hear more.

grounding: It shows a child using arms and fingers to show size and number, exaggerating the fish to share her excitement.

passage:
"Where's Sahil?"

"On the sofa. His cousin called him a crybaby at lunch."

Papa went in. "Sahil? What happened? Who said it? Why didn't you tell me? Are you hurt?"

Sahil pulled his knees up, tucked his chin and turned his face into the cushion.

"Let him be for a bit," Sangeeta said softly. She sat at the other end of the sofa with her tea and didn't say anything else.

After a while, Sahil's foot slid over to touch her leg.

"I'm here," she said.

"He laughed at me," he whispered.

qa.q: What did Sahil's cousin call him at lunch?
qa.a: A crybaby.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he tucked his chin and turned his face into the cushion?
qa.a: He was most likely hurt and ashamed after being teased, and wanted to hide. Papa's many questions may have made him feel even more crowded.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Sangeeta's quiet presence worked better than Papa's many questions, because it let Sahil come to her in his own time.

qa.q: How does Papa probably feel when Sahil curls up?
qa.a: Papa is likely worried and wants to fix things fast, which is why he asks so many questions at once.

grounding: It shows a child curling up after being teased and a quiet, non-intrusive presence working better than many questions.
